title: The present continuous
intro: So far every sentence has used **to be**. This unit brings in real verbs and the first verb tense, the present continuous `-(I)yor`: *Ne yapıyorsun?* (What are you doing?) *Kitap okuyorum* (I'm reading a book). It covers how to find a verb's stem, how to build the tense in the positive, the negative and the question, and when Turkish uses it.

sections.title: Gelmek, gel-: the infinitive and the stem

blocks.text: Dictionaries list Turkish verbs in the infinitive (*mastar*), which always ends in `-mAk`: *-mek* after a front vowel, *-mak* after a back vowel. *Gelmek* means **to come**, *okumak* **to read**.

Take `-mAk` off and you have the stem (*fiil kökü*), the part every other verb ending attaches to: *gel-*, *oku-*. This course writes stems with a hyphen. Most stems end in a consonant; some end in a vowel, and those behave a little differently in the present continuous.

items.en: to write: the stem is yaz-
to work: the stem is çalış-
to want: the stem is iste-
to learn: the stem is öğren-

blocks.text: On its own, the stem is also the command form for *sen*: *Gel!* (Come!), *Oku!* (Read!). You'll practise commands in [unit 12](gp-imperative).

*Yemek* is both the verb **to eat** and the noun **meal, food**: *Yemek yiyoruz* (We're eating a meal). Don't let it confuse you, and don't mistake nouns that happen to end in *-mek* or *-mak* for verbs: *ekmek* (bread), *parmak* (finger).

The present continuous (*şimdiki zaman*) is built in three pieces: the stem, `-(I)yor`, and the personal endings of **to be** you know from [unit 3](gp-copula-present): *gel-* + *-iyor* + *-um* → *geliyorum* (I am coming).

blocks.label: Present continuous
lines: ı, i, u, ü:   oku- → okuyor     yürü- → yürüyor
a or e:       anla- → anlıyor   bekle- → bekliyor

blocks.text: **The vowel before -yor.** After a consonant, `-Iyor` brings its own vowel, in four-way harmony with the stem: *geliyor*, *yapıyor*, *konuşuyor*, *görüyor*. After a stem ending in ı, i, u or ü, *-yor* goes straight on: *okuyor*. A stem ending in a or e drops that vowel, and the I of `-Iyor` takes its place, in harmony with the vowel before it: *anla-* → *anlıyor*, *bekle-* → *bekliyor*, *iste-* → *istiyor*.
**-yor itself never changes.** Its o doesn't follow harmony, so the endings after it always have u: *-um*, *-sun*, *-uz*, *-sunuz*, and *-lar* for **they**.

-(I)yor

blocks.text: **Three special verbs.** The one-syllable stems *ye-* (eat) and *de-* (say) become *yiyor* and *diyor*. And *git-* (go) and *et-* (do) turn their t into d before the vowel: *gidiyor*, *ediyor*, also in phrases with *etmek*: *dans ediyorlar* (they're dancing), *teşekkür ediyorum* (I thank you).
Only *gitmek*, *etmek* and a handful of rare verbs soften their t. Most verbs in t keep it: *yatıyor* (is lying down), *satıyor* (is selling).

A bare object, with no ending, means **a** or **some**: *Kitap okuyorum* (I'm reading a book), *Çay içiyoruz* (We're having tea). For **the** book, Turkish adds the accusative ending of [unit 8](gp-accusative).

**Negative.** Put `-mI-` between the stem and *-yor*: *gel-* + *-mi-* + *-yor* + *-um* → *gelmiyorum* (I'm not coming). The vowel of `-mI-` follows four-way harmony with the stem: *gelmiyor*, *yapmıyor*, *okumuyor*, *görmüyor*.

rows.en: he or she is not coming

blocks.text: The stem stays whole in the negative, since the negative suffix starts with a consonant: *beklemiyor*, *anlamıyor*, *gitmiyor* (no d: the t only softens before a vowel), *yemiyor*.

**Questions.** The particle `mI` comes after *-yor*, so it is always *mu*, and it carries the personal ending: *Geliyor musun?* (Are you coming?). **They** keeps *-lar* on the verb, and the particle follows it as *mı*: *Geliyorlar mı?*
The negative has a high vowel, never e or a: *gelmiyor*, not *gelmeyor*. And the ending goes on the particle, not on the verb: *geliyor musun?*, never *geliyorsun mu?*
`-(I)yor` does more than the English **-ing** form. It covers three jobs:

items: **What is happening now:** *Şu anda çalışıyorum* (I'm working right now).
**What is true these days**, a situation for a while: *Bu aralar Türkçe öğreniyorum* (These days I'm learning Turkish).
**What is planned** for the near future, with a time word: *Yarın geliyorum* (I'm coming tomorrow), *Bu akşam ne yapıyorsun?* (What are you doing this evening?).

blocks.text: It is also the normal tense for verbs of knowing, wanting and liking, which English puts in the simple present: *Anlıyorum* (I understand), *Biliyorum* (I know), *Çay istiyorum* (I want tea), *Seni seviyorum* (I love you).

items.en: Ali is working a lot these days.

blocks.text: French uses its plain present for all three jobs: je travaille, ces jours-ci j'apprends le turc, je viens demain. Turkish `-(I)yor` maps onto the French present far better than onto the English **-ing**.

For habits and general truths Turkish has another tense, the aorist (*Her sabah çay içerim*, I drink tea every morning), coming in [A2](gp-aorist-forms). In everyday speech `-(I)yor` is often used for habits too: *Her sabah çay içiyorum*.

summary: Verbs are listed in the infinitive `-mAk`: *gelmek*, *okumak*. Take it off to get the stem: *gel-*, *oku-*.
Present continuous: stem + `-(I)yor` + the endings of **to be**: *geliyorum*, *yapıyorsun*, *okuyor*.
Stems in a or e drop that vowel: *anlıyor*, *bekliyor*. *Ye-* and *de-* give *yiyor*, *diyor*; *git-* and *et-* give *gidiyor*, *ediyor*.
*-yor* never changes, so the endings after it always have u: *-um, -sun, -uz, -sunuz*.
Negative `-mI-` before *-yor*: *gelmiyorum*. Question: *geliyor musun?*, but *geliyorlar mı?*
`-(I)yor` says what is happening now, what is true these days, and what is planned: *Yarın geliyorum.*
